title: Pooled Warmth & Eviction Heuristics — Dedicated POC Playbook (Workshop Notes)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook from the November 2024 Solutions Eng workshop. Target audience: solutions engineers running Dedicated POCs who need deterministic latency at low unit cost. Focus areas: pool "warmth" (prewarmed GPUs / containers), eviction heuristics for reclaiming capacity, micro-batching thresholds, and simple cost estimates to share with customers during sales/technical calls.

Context / motivation:
- Customers want steady 95th/99th percentile latency while minimizing committed capacity for financial reasons.
- Typical POC pattern: bursty traffic with predictable peaks (business hours) and long idle tails overnight/weekends.
- Naive always-on reserved pools are wasteful; fully reactive autoscaling introduces cold-starts that break SLOs.
- Middle ground: small warm pool + eviction policies + transient burst buffers.

Key constraints assumed for heuristics:
- Model types: Llama2-13B-ish or open/flan variants; KV cache per request ~ 1–3GB depending on context length.
- GPU options commonly proposed in POCs: A10G (cost ~ $2.5/hr effective), A100-40 (≈ $6/hr), H100 (≈ $12/hr). Use MSRP-ish numbers for first-order comparables; vendor discounts vary.
- SLO targets typical in POCs: p50 < 150ms, p95 < 400ms, p99 < 900ms for short-chats (<= 256 tokens).
- Billing horizon for commitments: monthly/quarterly; POC length 2–8 weeks.

High-level recommended architecture for POCs:
1) Small warm pool sized to cover baseline concurrency (baseline = 20–40% of predicted peak).
2) Burst buffer: ephemeral warmers (on-demand prewarm to handle burst above baseline up to 1.5–2x peak).
3) Eviction tiers: soft-eviction (scale-down to baseline overnight), hard-eviction after sustained idle (24–72h) with snapshot/fast-rebuild hints.
4) Autoscale rules: combine queue length + tail-latency alarms + scheduled scaling for predictable windows.

Eviction heuristics (concrete):
- Warmth TTLs:
  - Active: last_request < 5m -> never evict.
  - Cool: last_request 5m–2h -> eligible for soft-evict (drain after current requests, keep a warm fraction).
  - Cold: last_request 2h–24h -> mark for hard-evict; release GPU but retain model artifacts in cache-tier (if available) to speed rehydrate.
  - Aged: last_request > 24h -> full reclamation; require full cold start on next use.
- Warm fraction policy: keep 10–25% of baseline as instantly available warm VMs/containers to avoid tail spikes when multiple concurrent cold starts happen.
- Eviction priority score (composed metric):
  score = 0.5 * idle_seconds_norm + 0.3 * (memory_pressure_norm) + 0.2 * (cost_weight)
  - idle_seconds_norm scaled 0..1 for 0..72h, memory_pressure_norm from 0..1 based on pool fragmentation, cost_weight a per-customer preference 0..1.
  (This is intentionally lightweight, implementable in a rules engine.)

Prewarm strategy details:
- Prewarm triggers: scheduled windows (cron), rolling window ahead of predicted hourly peaks, and predictive prewarms using last-week same-hour heuristics.
- Prewarm grain: start model process on GPU + load weights to VRAM + warm small synthetic requests to populate KV cache. Warm time measured experimentally: 30s–120s depending on model/device.
- Tradeoffs: aggressive prewarm reduces p99 but increases committed cost. Provide graphs/examples to customers showing marginal p99 improvement vs. $/hr.

Micro-batching and routing heuristics:
- For chat workloads with many short requests: enable micro-batching on 10–30ms window if user latency budget allows (useful to reduce per-token cost).
- Batch size selection: dynamic cap at 4–8 requests for p95-sensitive flows, up to 16–32 for background bulk-generation.
- Routing policy: route latency-sensitive routes to warm pool only; allow background routes to be routed to opportunistic/spot backends.

Simple cost model (example scenarios) — numbers for workshop discussion only:
- Assumptions: A10G = $2.5/hr; baseline concurrency 20 rps; average generation length 120 tokens; model throughput on A10G ~ 18 tokens/sec (per GPU) for given config; micro-batching improves effective tokens/sec by ~1.6x.
- Scenario A (always-on baseline of 2 GPUs): cost = 2 * $2.5 * 24 = $120/day => $3600/month. P99 ~ 200–350ms.
- Scenario B (1 warm GPU + burst buffer autoscale up to 4 GPUs): base = 1 * $2.5 * 24 = $60/day; burst delta depends on hours of peak. If peak 4 hours/day at +3 GPUs average: extra = 3 * $2.5 * 4 = $30/day. Total ~$90/day => ~$2700/month. P99 ~ 300–700ms depending on prewarm hit rate.
- Scenario C (baseline 0 warm, fully reactive): cost lower nominally but p99 spikes to multiple seconds due to cold starts — not recommended unless upstream client enforces long timeouts and workload is extremely spiky.

Cost sensitivity knobs to show customers:
- Increase micro-batching window by +10ms -> incremental 8–12% token throughput uplift -> lowers required GPUs.
- Enable 4-bit quantization (if model supports) -> reduces VRAM footprint -> allows more copies per GPU -> reductions in committed pool size.
- Adjust warm fraction down 5% -> immediate $/hr savings, but watch p99 drift.

POC runbook checklist (quick):
- Before POC: capture traffic profile (sample of requests, token lengths, per-route latency targets), sign baseline SLA for workshop.
- Day 0: deploy baseline warm pool (1–2 GPUs), run synthetic warmup scripts to measure warm time and p99.
- Day 1–3: run real-traffic pilot, collect p50/p95/p99, queue lengths, cold-start counts.
- Day 4–7: iterate autoscale rules (shorten/lengthen cooldowns, change prewarm heuristics) and present cost-latency tradeoff deck to customer.
- Post-POC: provide exportable model showing recommended warm pool sizing and expected monthly committed cost under three consumption scenarios.

Workshop notes / decisions taken during session:
- Consensus: keep baseline warm fraction at 15% for enterprise POCs unless strong traffic predictability exists.
- Action: engineering to prototype eviction score in staging by Nov 15; solutions-eng to test against 3 customer traces.
- Risk called out: customers with heavy long-context chat (>= 2k tokens) may invalidate quick warm heuristics due to large KV restoration times — flag during scoping.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can we persist partial KV checkpoints to S3 to allow faster rehydrate without full cold-start? (Eng to evaluate feasibility.)
- How to expose per-customer cost-vs-latency slider in Console for quick demos? (Product / Console owners).
- Investigate whether per-GPU pricing tiers should be surfaced as per-route cost-estimates in billing UI.

Appendix: quick CLI commands used in experiments (examples):
- preload script: python tools/prewarm.py --model llama-13b --gpu A10G --kv-warm 128 --synthetic-requests 10
- eviction simulator (local): ./tools/evict-sim --trace traces/customer_alpha.json --warm-frac 0.15 --ttl-cool 7200

Notes to self: capture screenshots of p99 vs warm fraction and add to final playbook. Keep this doc intentionally light on exact pricing; translate to a memo with customer-specific committed pricing once commercial terms are clear.

-- end of notes --
